newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-She tries, but Faye Dunaway can't shake diva image.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-She tries, but Faye Dunaway can't shake diva image.

text.p: She tries, but Oscar-winning actress Faye Dunaway still cannot shake her reputation as one of Hollywood's prima donnas.

Maybe this is why: When invited guests arrive at her swanky hotel room -- after she has told them she is ready to receive them and after they have seen the door is slightly ajar and walked in -- she asks them to wait. When they stand patiently in the foyer, she ignores them, prompting a question from one of the three: "Uh, did you want us inside or out?"
"Well, outside, of course," she snaps without turning. "Isn't that what 'wait' means?"

It is an unfortunate impression the 55-year-old Dunaway leaves because she is less a diva than, very simply, engaged by life, "hands on" about her work and finally "vulnerable," or so she says. "I think people think of me as being maybe domineering, maybe larger than life, maybe a diva," she said, sitting comfortably on an overstuffed couch, "but you know, those things aren't me at all."

Dunaway has built a 44-film, 29-year career playing strong women who mask a vulnerable quality in their character. The list of roles is as varied as the films are modern classics -- a gangster in "Bonnie and Clyde," a ruthless TV executive in "Network" -- for which she won the Best Actress Oscar for 1976 -- and the mysterious femme fatale in "Chinatown."
Her latest incarnation is Lee Hall Bowen, a Southern belle desperate to hide her past from Mississippi society in "The Chamber," the film adaptation of John Grisham's popular novel.
"It's a plum part, you know," she said of the Bowen character. "It has colour, variety and some growth."
In "The Chamber," Bowen is forced to relive her history as the daughter of a racist farmer who was convicted of killing two children in the bombing of a Jewish attorney's office.

After daddy is sent to jail, she manages to marry a wealthy man and become the consummate belle, entertaining society in her mansion, but all of her wealthy privileges cannot mask the secret pain of her childhood. When her nephew, played by Chris O'Donnell, comes to Mississippi to try to save Bowen's father (Gene Hackman) from the gas chamber, Bowen is forced to open the closet on all her old skeletons.

It is a difficult role for an actress because it requires a wide range of emotion, from sweet and sassy to cool and calculating to down-and-out drunk, Dunaway says. But she is known for playing multi-faceted and complicated roles, such as Joan Crawford in 1981's "Mommie Dearest."

In interviews, she fends off questions about what some critics called her over-the-top portrayal of Crawford, simply saying, "I think my performance was wonderful." She refuses to discuss the most recent controversy of her life, being cut from the Los Angeles stage production of Andrew Lloyd Webber's "Sunset Boulevard," saying terms of her legal settlement prevent her from doing so.

It is the characters she plays and her reputation as being demanding on the set that have led many people to characterise her as a prima donna, but she insists that is not the real Faye Dunaway. The Florida native who yearned to leave the South and dreamed of being an elegant actress of the stage and screen is like stars of old -- a cross between a lonely Greta Garbo and a business-minded Mary Pickford.

Like Garbo, she has been pegged as sexy and provocative but aloof. In reality she is more Pickford, who helped form United Artists film studio. Dunaway picks her own scripts, develops them and handles many of her own business affairs.

"Sometimes people have a very simplistic view of the complexity of people," she said. "They think if you are strong then you must be unfeeling. Quite the opposite is true. I'm strong, yes, but I'm sensitive."
